title: Lending Solutions Redesign
subtitle: Reinventing end-to-end lending for J.P. Morgan Private Bank — one origination flow across four regions, three products, and two request types.

meta.label: Company
meta.value: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, Wealth Management

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Product (multi-domain POs), Engineering, UX Research, Credit Middle Office

indexedSections.title: A private bank running on disconnected tools

value: J.P. Morgan Private Bank serves ultra-high-net-worth clients across 140+ countries, offering lending products like Securities-Based Lending and Custom Credit.

But behind every loan sat a broken workflow. To complete a single loan request, an Advisor had to jump between multiple disconnected applications — re-keying data, chasing manual handoffs with Credit Middle Officers, and relying on institutional memory to know what to do when.
I owned the redesign of the end-to-end lending experience, across two surfaces.

items.title: Loan Request App 3.0
items.desc: The origination surface where Advisors initiate and submit SBL, Custom Credit, and PLP tickets — new deals and amendments — across USPB, EMEA, APAC, and LatAm.

items.title: Lending Workspace
items.desc: The unified hub bringing every Private Bank lending tool under one roof.

blocks.value: The tools existed. The experience didn't.

indexedSections.title: People with no room for internal friction

blocks.value: My primary users were Advisors and Bankers serving UHNW clients who expect fast, accurate answers.

items.title: Time-starved
items.desc: Every minute with a client is high-stakes. Internal tooling friction is a direct tax on client service.

items.title: High-consequence
items.desc: A single ticket can move eight figures. An error isn't an inconvenience — it's a risk event.

items.title: Knowledge-gated
items.desc: Complex, multi-step, tool-dependent workflows that punished anyone without deep institutional knowledge.

blocks.label: Design principle
blocks.value: Remove the friction that wastes time — keep the friction that protects the client.

indexedSections.title: A variable matrix, not a form

value: The v1 experience was a flat, linear form: no conditional logic, no real-time feedback, no embedded guidance. Advisors were expected to already know what to fill in, when, and why.
But a loan request isn't one form — it's a combinatorial matrix.

blocks.value: That explodes into hundreds of possible states. Two problems compounded it.

items.label: Problem A
items.title: No single source of truth
items.desc: Each domain had its own Product Owner with limited cross-domain visibility — leading to conflicting requirements, overlapping asks, and three months of circular debate over whose process was the standard.

items.label: Problem B
items.title: No shared mental model
items.desc: Everyone pictured the lending space differently, so we kept arguing about fields when the real disagreement was about structure.

blocks.title: Map the whole space before touching a screen

value: Instead of designing screens, I first built a comprehensive information architecture covering every domain, product, and region — a single holistic view of the entire lending surface.
The IA's value wasn't aesthetic. It turned invisible disagreements into visible, pointable nodes. “Whose process wins?” became “which region owns this specific node?” — a solvable question.
I designed the space first, then the screens, so every later decision had a coherent home.

blocks.title: Unify the skeleton, localize the organs

blocks.value: The hardest tension surfaced immediately: how much to unify?

items.label: Fully global
items.desc: EMEA's mandatory compliance fields get cut. A non-negotiable red line.

items.label: Fully local
items.desc: We're back to four disconnected tools. Unification dies.

blocks.value: My decision: one shared flow structure, navigation, and mental model across all regions, with conditional logic dynamically injecting region-specific fields and disclosures inside each step. Advisors experience one product; the system quietly adapts underneath.

blocks.title: Lead by showing — a prototype that ended the debate

value: I could say “skeleton vs. organs,” but POs didn't buy an abstraction — they kept asking “is my field still there or not?”

So I stopped arguing and built an interactive prototype using LLM-assisted tooling. Select EMEA and the three compliance fields appear. Switch to USPB and they disappear, and the rest of the flow doesn't move.

blocks.value: Oh — my field wasn't deleted. It just doesn't exist in the other regions.

value: Three months of debate collapsed in a fifteen-minute walkthrough.
When consensus is missing and talk won't converge, a prototype isn't a deliverable — it's a decision-making instrument. It swaps “who's right” for “does this work.”

blocks.title: The friction I chose to keep

blocks.value: My first pass optimized for pure speed — auto-advancing, stripping confirmations. Then a senior Advisor, mid-walkthrough, said:
The seconds you saved me might let me submit a multi-million-dollar loan without ever seeing the collateral details.
That reframed everything. In finance, some friction is a bug; some friction is a feature.

items.label: Removed — bug friction
items.desc: Re-entering data, not knowing the next step — removed via conditional logic, inline validation, and embedded guidance.

items.label: Kept & hardened — prudent friction
items.desc: A deliberate, un-skippable confirmation of key terms and collateral before submission — kept and hardened, because it carries accountability and risk control.

blocks.value: I demoed both in the same prototype — this step is fast on purpose, that step is slow on purpose — so Product and Compliance saw that efficiency and prudence weren't in conflict. They were being deliberately separated.

value: I partnered with a UX Researcher to run sessions on the interactive prototypes directly with Advisors. These surfaced edge cases and workflow assumptions invisible in stakeholder reviews alone, which I synthesized back into iterative design improvements.

I then delivered pixel-perfect handoff across regional variants and product types — SBL, Custom Credit, PLP — with full edge-case and error-state coverage, and stayed embedded in engineering standups through implementation.

items.label: reduction in ticket completion time
items.desc: Removed bug friction without touching prudent friction.

items.label: Reduced NIGO rate
items.desc: Embedded tooltips and progressive disclosure cut submission errors and Advisor call-ins.

items.label: Adoption expanded EMEA → USPB
items.desc: One unified skeleton proved it could scale across two major markets.

items.label: Positive Advisor feedback at launch
items.desc: Credited the redesign with reducing friction and improving completion confidence.

blocks.value: The win wasn't trading prudence for speed — it was replacing wasted friction with necessary friction.

value: I joined by listening first — meeting triad partners, studying existing research, immersing in the design system — before moving into end-to-end ownership.

My biggest takeaway is a decision-making mindset: when a room can't agree in the abstract, the fastest path forward isn't more debate — it's a prototype people can touch, so the solution argues for itself.

That, to me, is senior design: not just crafting the interface, but using systems thinking and prototyping to help a room of conflicting stakeholders make a decision — and knowing which friction to fight and which to defend.
